description:
Project purpose

We are developing a smartwatch prototype connected to a computer-based control interface.

The system aims to:

Display heart rate, estimated blood oxygen saturation, and surface temperature.

Send an SOS notification through a physical button.

Show incoming alerts on the watch and provide vibration feedback.

Highlight spacecraft faults in red on the interface.

Explain faults through text and speech

At this stage, this is an educational demonstration prototype.
summary:
NEXORA is a prototype monitoring and communication system designed to demonstrate how astronauts could receive important information and alerts during space missions. Its interface brings together temperature monitoring, an SOS feature, messaging, and a spacecraft panel that highlights reported faults in red. The design also includes written and spoken alerts and customization options.

Our hardware prototype uses an ESP32 board, a DS18B20 temperature sensor, and a small vibration motor. A Python application is designed to display temperature readings and send vibration commands through a USB connection. This allows us to demonstrate how a warning on the screen could become a physical alert on a wearable device.

The project aims to make information easier to notice through visual, audio, and vibration feedback. Hardware testing and full integration are still in progress. NEXORA is an educational prototype; it is not connected to NASA’s operational communication systems or certified for medical or spaceflight use.
details:
Our project is called NEXORA SOFTWARE. We are developing a prototype that combines an astronaut interface, spacecraft fault displays, communication features, and a physical temperature and vibration system.

Below is a step-by-step explanation of our work, including what is ready and what still needs testing.

1. Project purpose

NEXORA aims to help users notice important information through visual, audio, and vibration alerts. We designed it around a space mission scenario, where astronauts need clear information about their surroundings, equipment, and communications.

2. Main interface

We created a website interface with a black-and-white default appearance. It brings together health information, spacecraft information, settings, and a watch-style display.

The preview includes example heart rate, oxygen, temperature, and step values. These example values are not measurements from our current hardware.

3. Spacecraft catalogue

We added a catalogue based on NASA’s publicly available spacecraft and space-related visual resources.

Users can browse and select different models. The catalogue contains 327 archive images, while representative component diagrams cover a smaller selection of vehicles and living modules. We did not create a detailed engineering model for every catalogue item.

4. Spacecraft fault display

We designed a system that highlights the reported location of a spacecraft problem in red.

For example, a demonstration incident can identify a problem with the power system or thermal control system. The interface then shows the affected section and explains the reported problem and its cause.

The component locations are illustrative. They are not verified engineering maps, and the system does not independently diagnose real spacecraft faults.

5. Written and spoken alerts

We added text explanations and speech features so users can read or hear important information.

The spacecraft panel can read an incident description aloud. This helps demonstrate how an astronaut could receive an alert without constantly watching the screen.

6. Customization

We added customization controls with at least 12 colour options and 12 pattern options.

Users can change the appearance to suit their preferences, while the initial design remains black and white.

7. SOS interface

We designed a prominent SOS control and a receiver screen to demonstrate an emergency notification workflow.

The intended flow is for a user to request help and for another person to receive and acknowledge the alert. The currently published HTML preview does not send real SOS notifications.

8. Communication features

The wider application includes work on messaging between users, contacts, and a simulated mission team.

We also planned command messages that could provide information about spacecraft faults. These features require the application’s server; they are not connected to NASA’s operational communication systems.

9. Wellbeing and accessibility

We added a wellbeing section with mood choices and supportive messages.

The interface also includes speech controls and Turkish, English, and German language options. These features aim to make the prototype easier to understand and use.

10. Wearable concept

We designed a watch-style interface as part of the project.

Our current physical setup is a breadboard prototype, not a completed smartwatch. It demonstrates some of the functions that could later be included in a wearable device.

11. ESP32 controller

We selected an ESP32 Lite board as the controller for the physical prototype.

Its job is to read the temperature sensor and control the vibration motor. Although the board supports Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, our current test setup uses USB communication with a Mac.

12. Temperature sensor

We used a DS18B20 temperature sensor.

The planned connections are:

Sensor connection

ESP32 connection

Power

3.3 V

Ground

GND

Data

GPIO4

A 4.7 kΩ resistor connects the data line to 3.3 V. The sensor is intended to demonstrate temperature changes, such as when someone holds its metal probe. It is not a clinical body-temperature measurement system.

13. Vibration motor circuit

We designed a motor circuit using a small vibration motor, an NPN transistor, resistors, a protection diode, and a separate two-AA battery supply.

The ESP32 sends the control signal through GPIO26. The transistor switches the motor’s current, while the batteries supply its power. The diode protects against the voltage spike produced when the motor switches off.

The transistor’s physical pin order and the completed wiring still need verification before powered testing.

14. ESP32 program

We wrote an Arduino program for the ESP32 that:

  • Reads temperature approximately once per second.
  • Sends temperature readings to the computer.
  • Accepts a V command to activate vibration for approximately half a second.
  • Accepts an S command to stop the motor.
  • Reports a sensor error when it cannot obtain a valid reading.

The timed motor stop runs on the ESP32, so an active vibration pulse can finish even if the computer stops sending commands.

15. Python control panel

We created a Python application for the Mac. It opens a local control panel in a web browser.

The panel lets users select the USB port, view temperature readings, and send a vibration test command. It also includes an optional 30 °C demonstration alert.

This threshold is for demonstrating the system, not for making medical decisions.

16. Demonstration mode

We added a separate mode for trying the Python panel without hardware.

In this mode, a slider changes a simulated temperature value. The screen clearly identifies the data as a demonstration. It does not operate a physical motor or prove that the hardware works.

17. Software packaging and tests

We organized the test system into NEXORA_MAC_TEST.zip, containing the Python application, ESP32 program, startup script, instructions, and tests.

Three automated software tests passed. They checked communication-message handling, alert behaviour, stale readings, disconnection handling, and parts of the local web interface.

These tests do not replace testing with the actual ESP32, sensor, and motor.

18. Arduino setup and troubleshooting

We helped configure Arduino IDE on the Mac.

The initial upload failed because Arduino Nano ESP32 was selected. After changing the selection to ESP32 Dev Module, the computer correctly identified the ESP32 chip.

A later upload failed while checking the flash connection. We suggested reducing the upload speed from 921600 to 115200 and checking the USB connection and external wiring. A successful hardware upload has not yet been confirmed.

19. Online website preview

We published the uploaded HTML preview and changed its access settings so other people can view it.

This makes the interface available through a web link. However, the published preview remains separate from the local Python hardware panel. Publishing the HTML did not activate real messaging, SOS delivery, or ESP32 communication.

20. Custom domain

We added nexora.site as a requested custom domain.

The connection is currently pending. Domain ownership and DNS records must be verified before that address can serve the website. Adding the domain to the hosting configuration did not purchase or register it.

21. Remaining work

The next steps are to:

  1. Complete the ESP32 upload successfully.
  2. Verify the circuit and test the temperature sensor.
  3. Test the vibration motor through the Python panel.
  4. Integrate the verified hardware connection with the main application.
  5. Test communication and SOS workflows between devices.
  6. Complete domain ownership and DNS verification for nexora.site.
